content: The implementation of health guidelines should be monitored at the levels of health services, regions, and countries. This monitoring should be based on clearly defined criteria and indicators that align with locally agreed-upon targets. In collaboration with the WHO’s Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) and Maternal, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA) departments’ monitoring and evaluation teams, data on the implementation of these recommendations at country and regional levels will be collected and assessed in the short to medium term. This evaluation aims to determine the impact of these recommendations on national policies within individual WHO Member States. Additionally, information on recommended indicators can be gathered locally through interrupted time series or clinical audits. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) suggests the following indicators for consideration: 1. The proportion of women undergoing cesarean sections who receive antibiotic prophylaxis, calculated as the number of women receiving antibiotic prophylaxis divided by the total number of women undergoing cesarean sections. 2. The proportion of women with preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) who receive antibiotic prophylaxis, calculated as the number of women with PPROM receiving antibiotic prophylaxis divided by the total number of women with PPROM. 3. The incidence of surgical wound infections among women undergoing cesarean sections, calculated as the number of women with surgical wound infections after cesarean sections divided by the total number of women undergoing cesarean sections. The first two indicators assess the use of evidence-based practices among women at higher risk of infection during childbirth, while the third indicator evaluates the effectiveness of the intervention. The proposed guideline will be updated five years after publication unless significant new evidence emerges that necessitates an earlier revision. The Steering Group will continue to monitor research developments in the area of maternal peripartum infections, particularly for questions where no evidence was found or where recommendations are based on low-quality evidence. New recommendations or changes to existing ones may be warranted as new evidence becomes available. Following the publication and dissemination of the guideline, any concerns regarding the validity of a recommendation will be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans for updating the recommendation. As the guideline approaches the end of its five-year validity period, the responsible technical officer, in collaboration with the Steering Group, will assess the currency of the recommendations and the need for new guidance on the topic. If concerns arise about the validity of a specific recommendation due to new evidence, the systematic review addressing the primary question will be updated. The existing search strategy used for the initial review will be applied, potentially by the same systematic review team or another team if the original team is unavailable. Any new questions identified during the scoping exercise at the end of the five-year period will undergo a similar process of evidence retrieval, synthesis, and grading in accordance with WHO standards for guideline development. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to be included in the updated guideline.
